articles.title: Brian Ortega Issues Statement After Pulling Out of UFC 331
articles.summary: Long-time UFC veteran Brian Ortega issued a statement after he was forced to pull out of the upcoming UFC 331 card.Ortega was set to fight Renato Moicano in...
articles.body:
Long-time UFC veteran Brian Ortega issued a statement after he was forced to pull out of the upcoming UFC 331 card.

Ortega was set to fight Renato Moicano in a rematch on the UFC 331 main card, but due to an injury, he was forced to withdraw from the bout.

With Moicano vs. Ortega 2 now off the card, Gable Steveson vs. Sean Sharaf takes its place on the main card.

Taking to his social media, Ortega issued a statement about why he was forced to pull out of UFC 331, sharing a photo of a cut that he received in training above his eye.

"This one hurts. I have to pull out of the fight because of the stitches in my eye. I'm on weight, I've been training my ass off, and this has honestly been one of the best camps I've ever had. I was really looking forward to fighting at home in Los Angeles in front of my family, friends, and everyone who's been supporting me. My next fight is in soon, so I'm getting right back to training. We've brought some new people into camp and I'm excited to show you guys a new side of me. Thank you to everyone who's been supporting me through all of this. I'll see you guys in November," Ortega wrote on his Instagram .

In his statement, Ortega said that fans can expect to see him fight again in November, so perhaps he will be rebooked for the UFC 334 card on November 14 at Madison Square Garden in New York City.

If that happens, then he won't be fighting against Moicano, as the Brazilian was rebooked to take on Tom Nolan in the main event of the Meta Apex card on Halloween.

Ortega may still get a top-15-ranked opponent like Moicano, but it's also possible that the UFC might give him someone unranked for his next fight instead, especially after he was forced to pull out of UFC 331. After all, it's not easy to get ranked opponents, and it's even harder after you withdraw from a fight.

articles.title: Former UFC Champ Henry Cejudo to Fight 'Euphoria' Actor Javon Walton on Misfits Boxing Card
articles.summary: Former UFC champion Henry Cejudo is going to face an actor from Euphoria in his boxing debut later this month.
articles.body:
Former UFC champion Henry Cejudo is going to face an actor from Euphoria in his boxing debut later this month.

Per ESPN's Brett Okamoto , Javon Walton will replace Nurideen Shabazz to take on Cejudo in the main event of the Sept. 26 Misfits Boxing show in Miami.

"I knew all along that Dean The B---- would back out, and so I am not surprised," Cejudo said in a statement to Okamoto. "But I have a new opponent now, who thinks he's a fighter, but Wanna will be playing another robot by the time I'm done with him."

Scorecard & Prize Money in Ryan Garcia's Win

Walton, who turned 20 on July 22, is best known for his role as Ashtray on the first two seasons of the HBO show Euphoria . He turned pro as a boxer in 2023 after signing with Jake Paul's Most Valuable Promotions.

In four fights as a professional, Walton has a 3-0-1 record with one win via TKO. The Sept. 26 bout will be his first appearance since defeating Anthony Mora in September 2025.

"Henry Cejudo is an Olympic gold medalist and a former UFC champion, so I know exactly the level of athlete I'm stepping in there with," Walton told Okamoto. "This fight came up out of nowhere and I stepped up without hesitation. I stay ready for moments like this. This is boxing, and this is my world."

Cejudo was originally going to challenge Shabazz, but Shabazz withdrew from the match due to an injury.

The 39-year-old Cejudo is one of 11 fighters in UFC history to hold championships in two different weight classes. He's one of four UFC fighters who was a simultaneous champion in two divisions, along with Conor McGregor, Amanda Nunes, Daniel Cormier

Cejudo won the UFC flyweight championship from Demetrious Johnson in 2018. He captured the vacant UFC bantamweight title by defeating Marlon Moraes in 2019.

The California native vacated the flyweight title in December 2019 to focus on competing exclusively at bantamweight. He vacated the bantamweight crown in May 2020 after announcing his retirement.

After a three-year absence, Cejudo returned to mixed martial arts in May 2023 to challenge Alljamain Sterling for the UFC bantamweight championship. He lost via split decision, kicking off a string of four consecutive defeats and leading to his second retirement after a loss to Payton Talbott at UFC 323.

Cejudo's MMA career ended with a 16-6 record, including eight wins via knockout.

articles.title: Guerra por ser el nuevo campeón del peso pesado: Hokit y Pereira piden a Gane
articles.standfirst: Tras la decisión de Tom Aspinall de dejar el cinturón vacante, los dos nombres más mediáticos del peso completo han pedido ser los siguientes retadores al título contra el francés
articles.summary: Tras la decisión de Tom Aspinall de dejar el cinturón vacante, los dos nombres más mediáticos del peso completo han pedido ser los siguientes retadores al título contra el francés
articles.body: Los últimos días en el peso pesado de la UFC están siendo un absoluto caos. En el día de ayer, Tom Aspinall anunció que dejaba vacante su cinturón indiscutido al haber recaído de su lesión ocular que le ha mantenido un año fuera del octágono. Por tanto, Ciryl Gane -hasta ahora campeón interino- se ha convertido de manera inmediata en campeón indiscutido. Al conocerse la noticia, la reacción del resto de retadores ha sido inmediara, y el cerco se ha acotado a dos nombres: Alex Pereira y Josh Hokit. El pasado 14 de junio, Pereira y Gane se enfrentaron en el UFC Casa Blanca por el cinturón interino, y fue 'Bon Gamin' el que finalizó a 'Poatan' para hacerse con el título en una noche histórica. Sin embargo, el peleador brasileño se quejó por una serie de golpes en la nuca que recibió por parte de Ciryl, y nada más conocerse que es el campeón indiscutido ha pedido una revancha inmediata por el cinturón en el UFC 334 que se celebrará en noviembre en el Madison Square Garden de Nueva York. "Tengo muchas ganas de que salga bien, quiero ganar ese tercer cinturón. Creo que he hecho muchas cosas en la UFC y me merezco tener esas opciones", dijo Pereira a UFC Brasil. El objetivo Alex es claro: vengarse de Gane y convertirse en el primer triple campeón de la historia de la UFC. Sin embargo, en el UFC Casa Blanca también hubo otro nombre que brilló con luz propia, y no es otro que Josh Hokit. El peleador estadounidense se ha convertido en uno de los nombres más mediáticos de la división en apenas cuatro combates, interpretando a un personaje díscolo que genera polémicas allá donde va. Eso sí, cuando se sube al octágono no se le puede reprochar nada. Ante Curtis Blaydes protagonizó uno de los combates del año, mientras que el pasado 14 de junio noqueó a Derrick Lewis para ganar enteros como próximo retador al cinturón. A pesar de que una revancha entre Pereira y Gane sería una idea más lógica, Hokit ha alzado la voz a través de su cuenta de 'X', donde ha pedido ser él el que se enfrente a 'Bon Gamin'. "Los aficionados se merecen un combate entre Gane y yo. Le daré a Ciryl lo que se merece. articles.title: Scott Coker confident Ki MMA 'will have a star' built through featherweight grand prix
articles.summary: Scott Coker is feeling pretty good about what will come from his new promotion's featherweight grand prix in 2027.
articles.body:
NEW YORK – Scott Coker is officially back and ready to build his new mixed martial arts promotion from the ground up.

On Monday during a news conference at Cipriani 25 Broadway, Coker revealed the name and details for his new company, which was first announced to be in the works in May. Ki MMA, the name stemming from the Japanese word "ki" meaning "spirit, mind, and energy," will be Coker's fourth promotion that he has either founded or led, along with Strikeforce, Bellator MMA, and Fight Night at the Tech.

Coker's latest project, backed by $60 million in funding, includes familiar names serving as Coker's right hand mend, including former Bellator matchmaker Rich Chou and media executive Peter Levin, who joined him at Monday's unveiling.

"This is gonna be a great journey, and I get to do it with a lot of familiar faces and a lot of friends," Coker told MMA Junkie, "and we're going to put together a company that I think is going to be strong, well built, and have the pillars that are going to sustain for years to come."

Ki MMA fights will take place in a ring, another nod to Japanese tradition, as opposed to a customary cage, and the idea is to identify up-and-coming talent that can be built into household names. The way to do this? Tournaments.

Starting in 2027, Ki MMA will host a 32-man featherweight grand prix, with eight fighters from each of the following continents: North America, South America, Asia, and Europe. Each continent will send one representative to the semifinals, and the tournament will conclude with the finalists having to partake in two fights in one night.

While tournaments are not normally part of the modern MMA landscape, it's a format that should help Ki MMA stand out and one Coker believes in deeply.

"I do feel strongly about tournaments building stars quickly," Coker said. "By the end of the year, we will have a star, and we will have a new champion. We might have two or three (fighters) that we really like. I really love the format, and I've always loved it. I feel like martial arts should be a tournament format, really. Look at Pride, look at K1, look at UFC. Yes, will the fighters have to dig deep because of fighting two times in one night at the end? That's going to be tough, but that's why you've got to have your ki together. You've got to dig deep. … It's the mindset and fighting through barriers."

In addition to the featherweight grand prix, Coker said Ki MMA will pursue available notable free agents – such as former Bellator title challenger Michael Page, who just fouught out his UFC contract – although he's not had any conversations.

articles.title: Why so few companies make aircraft windows
articles.summary: Few companies have the technology to make aircraft windows which are getting harder to make.
articles.body:
An industrial nightmare was brewing south of Los Angeles.

In late May, a chemical storage tank with more than 7,000 gallons of toxic material began heating up – fast. The tank belonged to GKN Aerospace, a company that supplies parts to the aviation industry, including aircraft windows.

As the temperature inside the shiny metal storage vessel rose, workers realised they had a problem. The tank was at risk of exploding, potentially showering nearby neighbourhoods with methyl methacrylate (MMA), a skin and lung-irritating compound used in plastics production.

The tank's temperature reached 100F (38C) – though possibly went higher - 100F was simply the maximum reading on the temperature gauge inside.

More than 50,000 residents of Garden Grove city were evacuated and fire crews began hosing down the tank in a bid to cool it. At one point, the vessel "actually bulged" according to the local fire chief.

Thankfully, no explosion occurred. Months later, in August, GKN and local authorities announced a $100m (£74m) programme to compensate residents evacuated during the incident. But production of aircraft windows at the site, which had been halted, is still not fully restored.

This has sent a minor shockwave through the aircraft manufacturing industry because GKN is one of surprisingly few companies, anywhere in the world, that make aircraft windows – highly engineered, safety-critical parts for planes.

Production at GKN's Garden Grove facility currently remains hobbled, at roughly 50% of normal, according to public statements by its UK parent company Melrose Industries. The aim is to have full production restored by 28 September. GKN declined an interview with the BBC.

"They're one of only a handful of suppliers – less than a handful, really – of critical windows," says Marisa Garcia, an aviation industry analyst. "One of the breaking points of supply chain in aviation is you have very few companies qualified to do something and, when something goes wrong, it really upsets the entire system."

Boeing tells the BBC it is "taking steps to mitigate any potential impacts", describing the shortfall in production as an "industry-wide" situation.

"We are supporting our supplier," a spokesman adds. An Airbus spokeswoman says, "We are closely monitoring and are seeing positive progress toward a return to normal."

It comes at a time when airlines "can't get new aircraft fast enough," says Mike Stengel of AeroDynamic Advisory, a consultancy. "They're holding on to aircraft for longer."

Even though there are just a few aircraft window-manufacturing firms in existence, it's hard for new competitors to emerge because of how regulated the industry is, adds Stengel. "It can take time to pivot to a new supplier."

This leads to a "balancing act" between plane-makers and the firms they rely on for various parts, Stengel says.

To find out what goes into the making of an aircraft window, I spoke to Jean-Eric Vermont, general manager of French company Saint-Gobain Aerospace.

"We focus mostly on commercial aircraft, regional aircraft and helicopters," he says. Vermont declines, though, to say how much market share his company has in aircraft windows – or transparencies, as they are known in the trade.

The oval-shaped windows in the cabin, next to passengers' seats, are typically made of plastic-based materials, says Vermont. "You start from a sheet of acrylic," he explains. "Then you cut to size, [to] give the shape."

A Saint-Gobain spokesman confirmed to the BBC that the company does not store or process MMA like GKN, but rather purchases sheets of polymerised MMA, or acrylic.

Aircraft manufacturers are increasingly ordering larger cabin windows, says Vermont, in order to offer passengers a wider view of the world outside. It's a selling point but it requires additional testing to ascertain whether the bigger windows hold up as well as the smaller ones.

Saint-Gobain tests its windows by exposing them to pressures many times what would be normal on an aircraft flying at altitude.

These acrylic-based cabin windows are usually made out of two layers or plies, and Saint-Gobain also performs tests to confirm whether the window will survive even if one of those plies gets damaged.

Cockpit windows, Vermont says, are "totally different".

They are generally made of glass, which is chemically reinforced by adding potassium to it. This involves swapping smaller sodium ions for larger potassium ions, which helps to fill out the molecular structure of the glass, meaning that when it cools during production, it compresses into an extra strong, tight formation as it cools.

Some of the latest aircraft feature cockpit windows that are also curved, to make the plane more streamlined, which improves fuel efficiency. But curved cockpit windows are challenging to make – the slightest distortion or defect is clearly visible to the pilot.

Quality control checks are used to ensure no such impediments exist in the final product.

All aircraft windows must be resistant to impacts but cockpit windows, at the front of the plane, are especially vulnerable to bird strikes, says Vermont: "The issue is not the speed of the bird, the issue is the speed of the aircraft."

Saint-Gobain uses numerical simulations and "physical tests representative of a sizeable bird impact" to test its windows against this threat.

"Typically, if you go through a hailstorm or if you hit a large enough bird, the external ply will crack," says Vermont. "The cockpit window is designed for that."

A London to Londonderry flight was recently affected by a cracked cockpit window . While a mid-air emergency was declared, the plane landed safely. "There can be [such] cases," says Vermont, though he adds that Saint-Gobain's windows have not been involved in any recently.

"You're obviously dealing with a surface that is interfacing with two very different environments," says Stengel. "That's why these are more highly-engineered products."

articles.title: Caroline Dubois sets course for undisputed championship fight with 'jealous, threatened' Alycia Baumgardner
articles.summary: With American rival Alycia Baumgardner challenging Elif Nur Turhan for IBF lightweight title, WBO and WBC champion Caroline Dubois wants to unify against WBA title holder Stephanie Han; Watch Elif Nur Turhan vs Alycia Baumgardner on November 9 live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Baumgardner will challenge Elif Nur Turhan for the IBF lightweight world title, live on Sky Sports in the early hours of Monday November 9.

Dubois, the unified WBC and WBO 135lb champion, expects to fight the winner for the undisputed crown but doesn't want to wait on the sidelines. She intends to add another belt to her collection and is targeting Stephanie Han, the WBA belt-holder, next.

"I want to become undisputed and I want to be involved in relevant fights. To unify the division is my dream right now. The only other champion [available] is Han and we'll just have to see if I can get it in before the end of the year. If not we'll have to go early next year," Dubois told Sky Sports .

"Hopefully we'll be unified world champion by the end of this year or early next. One belt away from becoming undisputed."

Dubois completed a successful defence of her titles when she beat Amelia Moore in Birmingham last month and immediately afterwards engaged Baumgardner in a furious war of words.

"She's most definitely intimidated by me. She's frightened of what I bring to the table. When she looks at me I know that she sees a younger, better, stronger, more talented, more everything better than her. Everything I do is just better than her. I feel like she's threatened by that," Dubois said.

"Everything that she has had to work so hard to get I've had it and I've achieved it in such quick succession. She's threatened, she's jealous. She's feeling a lot of emotions and all I can say is I hope she can focus herself, get that win [over Turhan] and we can find out who's the best.

"I hope she wins the fight. I'm going to be real upset if she doesn't win because I need to show her something," Dubois continued.

"Elif Turhan, the champion, versus Alycia Baumgardner, the contender, is going to be an awesome fight. I want the winner. I've made it very clear. I feel like I have been very vocal about the fact that I want to become undisputed.

"The path has revealed itself to me. The path has become clear now... So close, but so far."

Watch Elif Nur Turhan vs Alycia Baumgardner on November 9 live on Sky Sports .

articles.title: UFC 331: Muhammad Mokaev says ‘politics’ will not stop him pursuing return to the UFC
articles.summary: Muhammad Mokaev tells BBC Sport that he is still searching for answers about why he was cut by the UFC in 2024 and dreams of returning to the organisation.
articles.body:
It has been more than two years since Muhammad Mokaev was released by the UFC - and yet he is still searching for answers.

In July 2024 the Russian-born Briton had just stretched his winning run in the promotion to seven fights with a unanimous decision victory over Manuel Kape at UFC 304.

From the outside, Mokaev appeared to have it all.

Victory over Kape in Manchester had seemingly further cemented his place as a top contender in the flyweight division and a title shot appeared to be within his grasp.

But later that night UFC president Dana White made the shock announcement they would not be re-signing Mokaev.

It was initially suggested Mokaev's behaviour in the build-up to facing Kape – which included clashes with his Portuguese rival at the fighter hotel and again at the weigh-ins – may have influenced the UFC's decision.

"If we talk about behaviour, right - if I'm a bad guy, why would you let me fight seven fights and renew my contract twice?" Mokaev told BBC Sport.

"If I'm a bad guy in the company and organisation, they would cut me after one or two fights.

The flyweight, who moved to Britain as a refugee when he was 12 years old, believes his wrestling-heavy style was a contributing factor.

Mokaev won his UFC debut via submission in just 58 seconds before beating Charles Johnson by unanimous decision in his second bout.

He says the UFC text his manager after that victory over Johnson saying "he needs to stop wrestling - we don't want these decision guy".

"I have around a 60% finish rate in the UFC. Four out of seven fights were finishes against top guys," Mokaev said.

"I don't know what else I need to do to show them - I was 21 when I was fighting these veterans and now I'm much better and much stronger.

"From 21 to 23, I beat all these guys. Even Manuel Kape, and he is ranked number two right now. I really don't understand the politics. I really don't know. I wish I knew the full story behind everything."

'They basically wasted two years of my life'

You only need one look at Mokaev's record since July 2024 to understand how determined he is to make his way back to the UFC.

Few fighters on the planet have been more active than the flyweight, who has competed eight times over the past two years.

Since leaving the promotion, he has finished opponents with chokes, body kicks, head kicks and punches, while also winning titles in BRAVE CF and ACBJJ.

Yet it has not been enough to catch the attention of UFC matchmakers Hunter Campbell, Mick Maynard and Sean Shelby.

Although Mokaev is in a WhatsApp group with Campbell and Shelby, he believes the UFC is constantly moving the goalposts.

"Hunter made me a promise. They basically wasted two years of my life," Mokaev explained. "That's how I feel right now. I don't think what they are doing is right."

Mokaev says he was also offered $10,000 (£7,399) to compete in UFC BJJ, a Brazilian jiu-jitsu competition, against bantamweight champion Mikey Musumeci.

Despite finding the proposed fee deeply insulting, he was willing to face the five-time world champion if the UFC offered him a contract afterwards.

"They said, 'no, this is different. BJJ is different. This is different. We have other plans.' I told them where to go," said Mokaev, who admitted his response to the UFC contained several expletives.

When Joshua Van defends his flyweight title in a rematch with Alexandre Pantoja at UFC 331 in Los Angeles, California, on Saturday, there will be a sense of what might have been for Mokaev.

That is because Van, 24, became the first UFC champion born in the 2000s when he defeated Pantoja in December.

It was a feat that had long looked likely to be achieved by Mokaev after he signed with the UFC in 2021 and quickly soared through the ranks.

Only former UFC champions Demetrious Johnson (13) and Pantoja (eight) have recorded longer winning streaks in the flyweight division than Mokaev (seven).

It is why he remains steadfast in his belief that he is the best flyweight in the world and that he will one day have UFC gold around his waist, even if it comes later than he anticipated.

"The way I'm going to compete and keep winning, eventually they're going to send me there," Mokaev said.

"Back then I said, 'the best fight the best.' But it doesn't matter what happens with the situation, I think I'm the best flyweight in the world and I deserve to fight the best."

It is also part of the reason he has decided to sign one-fight deals rather than committing to longer-term contracts.

There have been more lucrative, multi-fight contracts offered to Mokaev since 2024, though he will only consider signing them if the UFC's stance on his return does not soften.

One of those offers came from the Professional Fighters League (PFL) to fight in its bantamweight division, as the promotion does not currently have a men's flyweight division.

Mokaev says he would be tempted to put pen to paper if the PFL created a 125-pound division following its merger with Jake Paul's Most Valuable Promotions in July.

"I want to stay active because I'm still young. I just turned 26. Most people start their careers at this age," Mokaev said.

"I'm going to do what's best for my family."

articles.title: Michael Venom Page and the 5 UFC Stars That Should Jump to MVP MMA
articles.summary: By now you've surely heard the news: Michael "Venom" Page has completed his UFC contract, and the promotion will not be making him another offer.
articles.body:
By now you've surely heard the news: Michael "Venom" Page has completed his UFC contract, and the promotion will not be making him another offer.

Page's departure from the UFC is not really surprising—but also a little surprising, depending how you look at it.

On the one hand, the former Bellator star is now 39 years old, and responsible for some of the most dreadful UFC fights we've seen in recent years, notably his recent decision win over Nursulton Ruziboev, which looked like a sparring match. Based on that, he's obviously not a guy the UFC would want to keep around, especially given the high price tag he surely comes with.

At the same time, Page's UFC record sits at 5-1, spanning two divisions, with his lone loss coming in a close fight against recent title challenger Ian Machado Garry. So, even at 39, he's clearly still elite. We also know that, despite the sedative quality of most of his UFC fights, he's capable of some of the most extreme violence you'll ever see in a ring or cage, like his infamous, skull-cracking KO of Evangelista Santos. Considering all that, it's a shame the UFC didn't give him another chance to live up to his obvious potential.

The good news, at least as far as Page is concerned, is that he is unlikely to have much trouble finding a new home. In fact, he has seemingly already been welcomed to Jake Paul's MVP MMA promotion, which is set to kick off in earnest next year, following its absorption of the Professional Fighters League.

For all his flaws, Page is just the kind of fighter Paul will be looking to align himself with next year: legitimately talented in the cage, and capable of drumming up plenty of interest outside of competition too. Of course, the enigmatic Brit is not the only UFC star to tick those boxes. The UFC roster is full of fighters that Paul would surely be taking a serious look at, were they not locked up in airtight contracts.

Here are five other fighters we could eventually follow Page to Paul's upstart MMA promotion.

Tom Aspinall is now the former UFC heavyweight champion—but that's sure not his fault.

Aspinall held the division's undisputed title until very recently, and were it not for factors outside his control, could have kept his seat on the throne for years to come. Unfortunately, his last fight ended prematurely when he was poked in the eye multiple times by reigning interim champ Ciryl Gane, and the injuries he suffered as a result have kept him out of action since—and will do so for the foreseeable future. As a result, Aspinall decided—or was perhaps forced—to vacate his title and let the division move on while he attempts to get back into fighting shape.

Obviously, the real tragedy of this whole saga is that one of the best heavyweights we've ever seen in the Octagon is missing years of his prime due the mistakes of his last opponent. However, another unfortunate outcome of all of this is that it has clearly soured the relationship between Aspinall and UFC CEO Dana White, who has not been shy to criticize the former champ over the last year.

Their relationship became so strained that Aspinall signed with White's chief rival, Eddie Hearn.

In the time since signing Aspinall, Hearn has repeatedly criticized the former champ's UFC contract, going so far as calling it a " disgrace ." That, understandably, supercharged rumors that Aspinall may look to get out of his contract, and take his career elsewhere.

That would certainly be easier said than done, as UFC contracts are notoriously bulletproof, and Aspinall's isn't over yet. At the same time, leaving the UFC would open up some very interesting opportunities for him, namely a deal with MVP.

Paul's upstart promotion would surely pay him well, if only for the optics of treating him better than the UFC. They could also find him some very compelling opponents, namely former UFC champ Francis Ngannou, who left the promotion due to his own issues with White several years back, and picked up a devastating KO win over Philipe Lins on MVP's first MMA show earlier this year.

Arman Tsarukyan is clearly one of the best lightweights in the UFC. Unfortunately—and despite big wins over Charles Oliveira and Dan Hooker—a crack at the division's title has so far eluded him.

That's largely his own doing, as he can't seem to stay out of trouble outside the cage, and is clearly seen as a bit of a liability by UFC brass. He's also spent most of free time doing anything but fight for the UFC, competing RAF wrestling every few weeks, and collaborating with streamers and influencers almost daily, which gives the impression he's a little distracted.

At this point, the UFC's decision-makers clearly have so little faith in him that they won't even guarantee him a title shot if he beats fellow contender Mauricio Ruffy at UFC 331 this Saturday.

Of course, that's not to say it won't happen. If Tsarukyan beats Ruffy impressively, and makes a sincere commitment for showing up for a title fight, he might get the opportunity. At the same time, it's possible that his constant antics and apparent disinterest in actually fighting have already doomed him. He's certainly right that, if he loses to Ruffy, he probably won't ever get the opportunity.

If a title shot continues to elude Tsarukyan, and he's able to get out of his UFC contract, he'd be a great fighter for MVP to sign. That's first and foremost because he is absolutely elite, and like Page and Aspinall, would add immediate credibility to the promotion's already strong roster. Yet he will also appeal to the promotion because he's—for lack of a better term— extremely online. He is always followed by cameras, always streaming, always collaborating with influencers of Paul's ilk, and basically always in the headlines.

You had to know Paulo Costa would be on this list.

The Brazilian, a former middleweight title challenger and now a top light heavyweight contender, has bumped heads with UFC brass countless times over the years, and asked for his release from the promotion as recently as last week .

Like most popular, relevant fighters, the UFC is very unlikely to grant Costa a premature release from his contract. He's still valuable to them, and more importantly, would be valuable to their competition—like MVP.

Of course, that's exactly why a guy like Costa is so comfortable asking for his UFC release. For all the big opportunities that exist for him as a member of the UFC roster, he'd have no difficulty finding big fights outside the Octagon.

He would almost certainly get a cushy offer from MVP, for just the same reasons Tsarukyan would. On the one hand, despite some tough losses in recent year,s he recently reestablished himself as an elite fighter with a vicious win over Azamat Murzakanov. On the other, he is as active on social media as any fighter in the sport. In other words, he knows how to promote himself and engage with fans—something we know Paul and his team appreciate.

MVP would also have no trouble matchmaking for Costa, as they'll inherit a solid lineup of middleweights and light heavyweights from the PFL, such as Costello Van Steenis, Johnny Eblen, Impa Kasanganay, Bryan Battle, and Corey Anderson. He could even find himself in a blockbuster scrap with Paul, who has been teasing his MMA debut for years.

Brazilian lightweight Renato "Money" Moicano is not quite as elite Tom Aspinall or Arman Tsarukyan, or as popular as Paulo Costa. However, he undeniably high-level, and has developed a cult following, particularly in his home country, where is a very popular streamer. In other words, he's just the kind of fighter MVP would love to sign, both for the way he'd legitimize the quality of their roster, and help drum up interest in their events.

Granted, Moicano has never really butted heads with the UFC the way Aspinall or Costa have. Still, he's had his share of gripes with the promotion, oftentimes about the fights they offer him, such as his recent win over Chris Duncan . So, while leaving the UFC is probably not his first choice, it's probably something he would do if he was paid well for big fights.

MVP could definitely make that happen for him. They have the bankroll to rival or even surpass what he's paid by the UFC, and have plenty of elite lightweights for him to tangle with. Even if they don't re-sign Usman Nurmagomedov, they could set Moicano up with the likes of Alexander Shabliy, Gadzhi Rabadanov, and Paul Hughes. Those would all be very high-level matchups that would both challenge the Brazilian veteran, and add serious legitimacy to any MVP broadcast.

At his best, Jorge Masvidal was one of the top welterweights in the UFC, and one of the most popular fighters in the sport. That was when he was beating the likes of Darren Till, Ben Askren, and Nate Diaz, and battling Kamaru Usman for the welterweight title.

Following a string of losses from 2020 to 2023, Masvidal took a break from the UFC for a boxing rematch with Diaz, which he lost by decision. That left him winless in any combat sport since he beat Diaz in the Octagon in 2019, which obviously isn't great, especially considering he's now in his 40s.

Despite all that, Masvidal is adamant he is still under contract with the UFC, and that he and the promotion are hard at work ironing out the details of his Octagon return.

While that's definitely possible, it seems highly unlikely. It's more likely that's he's either misinformed, or naive. It's simply very hard to believe that the UFC would be willing to give him another opportunity, in light of his recent results, his age, and his price tag. Even if he is used to be a star. Even if he is still under contract.

That said, MVP would probably throw him a bone.

While Paul and co. will definitely be looking to bolster their roster with elite, relevant talent—like Aspinall and Costa—we also know they have no objection to squeezing the last dregs of juice out of fading MMA legends. Just this year, they did so with the likes of Ronda Rousey, Gina Carano, and Diaz on Netflix—to great success. They could surely find use for Masvidal in similar contexts, and have the money and platform to make him feel like the big deal he once was. It may not be exactly what he had in mind for the twilight of his career, but it beats hanging around the UFC like a party guest who has overstayed his welcome.

articles.title: James DeGale admits George Groves rivalry still makes him 'cringe' as he prepares for his comeback
articles.summary: James DeGale says his heated dispute with George Groves on Sky Sports show 'Ringside' is 'part of my journey'; the former world champion returns to the ring this month against Marcus Portman; DeGale has urged Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua to finally agree a lucrative 'farewell' fight
articles.body:
DeGale had an entertaining war of words with his fellow Londoner before they settled their dispute in a 2011 grudge fight as Groves emerged victorious by split decision at The O2 Arena.

Despite this early setback, DeGale would go on to become a two-time world super-middleweight champion, although the 40-year-old is still regularly reminded about his lively dispute with Groves on Sky Sports show 'Ringside.'

Speaking to Dev Sahni, Groves said: "It's a classic. I cringe when I watch that [clip of himself and Groves], but it's a classic.

"That's me at the age of 25. Brash, cocky, [wearing] Dolce and Gabbana.

"It's raw, thinking I was the man, but that's just a part of my journey."

DeGale defeated Andre Dirrell to secure the IBF title in Boston in 2015, while he also defeated Lucian Bute in Quebec and then battled to a thrilling draw with Badou Jack in New York.

But the Olympic gold medallist fears he is only remembered for losses against Groves and Chris Eubank Jnr on British soil.

"That Groves one was close. I can't argue. A lot of people thought I won. A lot of people thought he won," said DeGale.

"And then the Eubank one was just a mess.

"That's probably why the fans don't see me as one of the best, because of my losses against British opponents, but they don't realise that I had better wins than them.

"Let's be real, [Andre] Dirrell, was a quality amateur. He beat Carl Froch but didn't get the decision, it was close though. He was a bronze medallist in the Olympic Games, he would have beaten George and Chris.

"Bute had like 13 title defences. I had the war with Badou Jack. Even before that, [Marco Antonio] Periban, [Rogelio] Medina [Luna], Brandon Gonzalez."

DeGale is returning from retirement to face Marcus Portman in Wolverhampton on September 26, over seven years since his last fight against Eubank in which he says injuries severely hampered his performance.

Britain's current biggest rivalry between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua could finally be settled in December, with The Principality Stadium in Cardiff and Wembley Stadium being considered as potential venues.

"It's egos, boxing politics. I'm not too sure, it's a bit of a mess," said DeGale when asked about the Fury vs Joshua saga.

"You would think it would be in England, a nice farewell for AJ and Fury.

"It looks like they are coming to the end now.

"Get a £100m each and then run, say 'thank you, you've been brilliant, and then later.'"

articles.title: El durísimo ataque de Nate Diaz a Ilia Topuria: "Es un saco de boxeo"
articles.standfirst: El ex peleador de la UFC ha criticado a 'El Matador' para prolongar un beef que lleva mucho tiempo vigente
articles.summary: El ex peleador de la UFC ha criticado a 'El Matador' para prolongar un beef que lleva mucho tiempo vigente
articles.body: Nate Díaz se la tenía guardada a Ilia Topuria. 'El Matador' dijo hace un tiempo que el legendario ex peleador de la UFC era un saco de boxeo después de varias declaraciones cruzadas, y el estadounidense se ha tomado la justicia por su cuenta aprovechando la derrota del peleador hispanogeorgiano en el UFC Casa Blanca ante Justin Gaethje con unas declaraciones que traerán cola. El pasado 14 de julio, Ilia cayó ante Gaethje después de que su esquina parase el combate al finalizar el cuarto asalto. 'El Matador' perdió el invicto y el cinturón de peso ligero y acabó con la nariz, los dos orbitales y el pie fracturados, algo que ha aprovechado Nate para lanzar su ataque en una entrevista con MMA Fighting donde no se ha guardado nada. "Es patético, es un saco de boxeo. Me llamó saco de boxeo, pues él es un *** saco de boxeo", afirmó el menor de los Hermanos Díaz, que no parece tener una buena relación con Topuria. De hecho, no es la primera vez que Nate arremete contra Ilia, puesto que hace unos meses le calificó de "idiota" a través de sus redes sociales. Es más, Topuria nunca había hablado mal de Nate hasta que el estadounidense se metió con él y dijo que quería enfrentarle en el octágono en un futuro. Obviamente, el peleador hispanogeorgiano no se mordió la lengua. "Me encantaría pelear con Nate Díaz. Un saco perfecto, de los que me gustan. Tiene un estilo bastante bueno para que uno luzca. Da show, da espectáculo... Y al mismo tiempo es un saco perfecto. Un saco que habla y vende", dijo 'El Matador'. Al tiempo, Nate fue preguntado de nuevo por Topuria en una entrevista con Ariel Helwani, afirmando que ""Le daría una paliza de la ***. Este idiota es un imbécil. Mides un *** metro y medio. Oye, chico, te voy a dar una cachetada que te voy a sacar la ***". No se tomó nada bien las palabras de Ilia, y parece ser que el tiempo no ha curado la herida. Lo que está claro es que esa pelea entre ambos jamás se dará, ya que Díaz ya no pertenece a la UFC y hace tiempo que está lejos de su mejor nivel. Sin embargo, no sería raro ver a Ilia atacándole en un futuro si le preguntan por estas declaraciones, ya que no es la primera vez -ni seguramente sea la última- que el estadounidense busca agitar el avispero.

articles.title: WOW FC volverá al Roig Arena el próximo mes de noviembre
articles.summary: Será con WOW 34
articles.body: El próximo 21 de noviembre, la mejor liga de MMA de España volverá a Valencia y al Roig Arena. WOW FC ha anunciado que su evento WOW 34 tendrá lugar en el espectacular pabellón ubicado en la Capital del Turia. Será el segundo evento del año para WOW FC en dicha localización. El primero, el pasado mes de abril, ya fue un éxito al convertirse en el evento con mayor asistencia de público en la historia de las MMA españolas: más de 13.000 espectadores acudieron para ver el último combate de la leyenda Enoc Solves. La gran noticia, anunciada oficialmente hace unas semanas por la Generalitat, es que podrán asistir menores a dicho evento por primera vez. Y es que la Generalitat Valenciana ha anulado la normativa que impedía el acceso de menores a eventos de MMA como público. Ahora los menores de 18 años podrán estar presentes en eventos como WOW 34 acompañados por sus padres o tutores legales o bajo autorización si tienen 16 o 17 años. Está por anunciar, sin embargo, el cartel y los combates principales para dicho evento. Ese mismo mes, en noviembre, se espera que WOW FC tenga un evento en Madrid.
